results.title: Calibration and data-analysis routines for nanoindentation with spherical tips
results.content: For example, in certain materials, indentation using tips with large radii results in stress–strain curves with a hardening coefficient similar to that of uniaxial tests, while data obtained using indenters with smaller radii display an indentation size effect e.g., [5, 5581–5593 (2006). In this contribution, we test, integrate, and adapt several published strategies for calibration of spherical tip shape and machine stiffness, and implement a routine to calibrate the effective radius and machine stiffness using purely elastic indentation data collected on materials with varying elastic moduli. Alternatively, using data from fully elastic experiments in materials with a wide range of elastic moduli, optimum values of \(R_\text{eff}\) can be simultaneously determined alongside other variables (e.g., machine stiffness) with the constraint that \(R_\text{eff}\) is as constant with depth as possible e.g., [10, 1170–1185 (2008). In Fig.1, we display the reported elastic load–displacement curves in the reference materials collected with a tip with nominal radius \(R_\text{n} = 10 \; \upmu\)m, and mark the load and displacement used in Eq.8 with a dashed horizontal line. Summary of results for effective radius determined as the slope of a line fit through data calculated as the subtraction of elastic load–displacement curves at the same load in different reference materials following the method of Li et al. Although using the load-dependent \(R_\text{eff}\) in Fig.4(a) results in better agreement with the reported data, there is still some mismatch in the displacements, which corresponds to \(h_\text{err}\) and which we attribute to the stiffness of the machine-tip pair. In “Calibrations on materials with known moduli” section we determined that two key parameters (the effective radius and machine stiffness) are needed for each combination of machine and indenter tip (Fig.6) to calculate the Young’s modulus and stress–strain curves using load–displacement data. Moreover, Eq.23 implemented with corrected values for \(h_\text{c}\) and \(R_\text{i}\) results in essentially constant values for Young’s modulus, even after yield that are in agreement with previously published values for the tested materials e.g., [3. These improvements of the spherical nanoindentation technique are critical for refining the measurement and corrected values of the contact stiffness, given the importance of this measurement to the extraction of stress–strain curves, calculation of Young’s modulus, and analysis of pop-ins e.g., in Berkovich nanoindentation [43, 2137–2153 (2021)")].

results.title: Discrete-Direct Model Calibration and Uncertainty Propagation Method Confirmed on Multi-Parameter Plasticity Model Calibrated to Sparse Random Field Data
results.content: A discrete direct (DD) model calibration and uncertainty propagation approach is explained and demonstrated on a 4-parameter Johnson-Cook (J-C) strain-rate dependent material strength model for an aluminum alloy. The J-C model is calibrated to particular combinations of the data curves to obtain calibration parameter sets which are then propagated to “Can Crush” structural model predictions to produce samples of predicted response variability. (Such suitability is a matter of expert judgment, hopefully informed by model validation determination of predictive accuracy of the model and parameter values tested at other than the calibration conditions.) The four prediction results in the figure are processed with specialized sparse-sample 1D UQ techniques (as described and demonstrated in this paper) to obtain reliably conservative but not overly conservative estimates of response variability and related statistical quantities. Another principal contribution of the paper is a methodology for appropriate coordination of replicate tests to sample the random field at multiple strain rates and appropriately combine the data curve realizations to calibrate the model and propagate the variability information forward. Section 2 describes the 4-parameter Johnson-Cook (J-C) material strength model and its calibration to trial sets of random function data (force–displacement curves) from sparse uni-axial tension “tests” (virtual) at different strain rates. For the calibration-UQ test problem, random realizations of the J-C parameter values and Eq. 1 (using reference strain rate ε˙p _ ref = 0.00016/sec) can be used in device-level structural response simulations to determine material variability related component response variability. The two values of each QOI are random realizations of Can Crush response; they are based on a particular calibration treatment using the four random F-D curves from virtual tests of four material samples derived from four random parameter sets A _i_, B _i_, C _i_, n _i_ (i = 1,4). The 40 calibrations use F-D curves generated from virtual tests at strain rate 10/sec taken from A _i_, B _i_, C _i_, n _i_ parameter sets _i_=1 to 20 of the 100 sets discussed in Sec. 2 that underlie the reference truth Can Crush QOI variability.
